newsitem.title: CHINA: China gun runners to U.S. jailed for up to 14 years.
newsitem.headline: China gun runners to U.S. jailed for up to 14 years.

text.p: A Chinese court has sentenced four people to prison terms of up to 14 years for smuggling into the United States the largest cargo of contraband automatic weapons in U.S. history, state media said on Saturday.

The gun smuggling ring, uncovered early last year, was initially reported to involve China's two largest government-run munitions merchants and caused huge embarrassment to Beijing at a time when Sino-U.S. ties had chilled over Taiwan.

China had vowed to punish those it said exported the firearms without approval, and the court said the weapons were smuggled by a gun-running ring that included employees of China's huge state munitions merchant, China North Industries Corp (Norinco).
The case was initially reported to involve both Norinco and China's other major government-run arms merchant, Polytechnologies Ltd, headed by a son-in-law of the late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

The Dalian City Intermediate People's Court handed down a 14-year sentence against Qi Feng, former manager of Duoweidi Science and Technology Co Ltd in Beijing, for illegally exporting the firearms to the United States, the China Daily said.
The court in the northeastern port city jailed three others, Lu Yilun, Qin Qixiu and Guo Chengkun, employees of Norinco, for three and four years for dereliction of duty.
U.S. federal agents last May seized the 2,000 AK-47 rifles and 4,000 ammunition magazines, with a street value of $4 million, the biggest haul of smuggled automatic weapons in U.S. history.

The court ruled that in July, 1995, Qi and Hammond Ku, a Taiwanese citizen and U.S. resident alien, jointly schemed to buy disassembled rifles in China for resale in the United States, state media said.
Qi contacted Qin, an employee of the Norinco's Dalian office, to seek customs clearance to export gun parts to the United States under Norinco's name, the China Daily said.
Qin agreed and Lu, assistant to Norinco Dalian's general manager, approved the deal without referring to higher authorities. Guo helped.
The ring used a U.S. import licence for rifle parts as well as counterfeit Chinese documents to export the weapons to the United States under Norinco's name in February 1996, it said.
The firearms were seized by federal agents and seven people in northern California, including Ku, were arrested and charged with involvement in the ring, U.S. reports said.

U.S. authorities said last year that Ku served as middleman in extensive negotiations between undercover U.S. agents posing as arms traffickers and two U.S.-based representatives of the Chinese munitions companies.

Federal agents said the suspects in the case had offered to sell undercover U.S. agents yet more sophisticated weapons, including hand-held rocket launchers, mortars, anti-aircraft missiles and even tanks.
Qi, formally arrested on December 18, 1996, earned 340,000 yuan ($40,900) as well as a certain amount of U.S. dollars from the deal, the China Daily said.

"Qi Feng, who had turned a blind eye to Chinese law and engaged in the illicit purchase and export of guns, had seriously endangered public security and was guilty of trading guns illegally," it quoted the court as saying.
